analogy.p: Think of the particles as pupils. **Kinetic energy** is how fast they are running about; the **temperature** is the average running speed. **Potential energy** is like pupils being held together by elastic bands: pulling them apart stretches the bands, storing energy. **Internal energy** is the total of all the running energy plus all the stretched-band energy for every pupil. Adding energy can make the pupils run faster (temperature rises) or stretch the bands (state changes). It breaks down because pupils choose their speeds, while particles' energies change through collisions and are not independent.

bullets: Energy stored by the particles is the system's **internal energy**.
A hot cup of tea and a cold cup of tea of the same mass differ in internal energy even though both are stationary on a table.
Internal energy is stored in the **thermal store** (the energy store changed by heating) in energy transfer diagrams.
Energy can be transferred to a system by **heating** (thermal energy transfer, e.g. a heater), by **doing work** (e.g. electrical or mechanical work), or by radiation.
The energy of the whole object (moving or lifted) is separate from its internal energy.
Always link to the **particle model**: the particles are in constant motion and attract one another.
core.h: What is a system and where is energy stored?
core.p: A **system** is the object or group of objects you are studying. In this topic the energy of a system is stored inside it by the **particles (atoms and molecules)** that make it up. This stored energy is not the same as the energy of the whole object moving (that is kinetic energy) or being high up (gravitational potential energy): it is the energy hidden in the random motion of, and forces between, the particles.

bullets: Internal energy = **total kinetic energy** of all particles + **total potential energy** of all particles.
**Kinetic energy** comes from the random movement (vibration, translation) of the particles.
**Potential energy** comes from the **forces of attraction between particles** and their separations; pulling particles apart against the attraction increases potential energy.
Internal energy is a property of the whole system, so a bath of warm water has more internal energy than a cup of water at the same temperature.
It is measured in **joules**; do not confuse it with temperature (measured in °C) or 'heat'.
**Common error:** forgetting to mention both kinetic AND potential energy.
core.p: The AQA definition you must learn word for word: **internal energy is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up a system.** Both words 'total' and 'all' matter: it is the sum over every particle, not the energy of one particle. It is measured in **joules (J)**.

bullets: Higher temperature means a higher **average kinetic energy** per particle.
Doubling the number of particles at the same temperature doubles the **total** kinetic energy but not the temperature.
This is why a bath of water at 40 °C has far more internal energy than a cup of water at 40 °C: same temperature, more particles.
In a solid, the kinetic energy is the energy of **vibration**; in liquids and gases it includes movement from place to place.
At the same temperature, particles of different substances have the same average kinetic energy, but different masses, so different speeds.
core.h: Kinetic energy of the particles and temperature
core.p: The kinetic energy of the particles depends on how fast they move or vibrate. The **temperature** of a substance is related to the **average kinetic energy** of its particles: the hotter the substance, the faster its particles move. If you add energy and the particles speed up, the temperature rises.

bullets: Solid to liquid to gas: potential energy increases because the particles are separated against the forces of attraction.
In an ideal gas the forces between particles are negligible, so the internal energy is essentially all kinetic energy.
The energy needed to separate particles (change potential energy) is supplied from the surroundings during melting and boiling.
When a gas condenses or a liquid freezes, potential energy **decreases** and the energy is released to the surroundings.
**Do not say** the particles 'break the bonds inside molecules': only the forces **between** particles are overcome.
core.h: Potential energy of the particles and bonds
core.p: Particles in solids and liquids attract each other. To pull them further apart you have to do work against this attraction, which increases their **potential energy**. In a solid the particles are close and the potential energy is lowest; in a gas they are far apart and the potential energy is highest. Potential energy changes therefore happen when a **substance changes state**.

bullets: **Temperature rise:** the energy goes mainly into the **kinetic energy** of the particles, so they move faster.
**Change of state:** the energy goes into the **potential energy**, overcoming forces between particles; the temperature stays constant.
If the system is cooled, the internal energy **decreases**: either the temperature falls or a gas condenses or a liquid freezes.
At any moment a system may be doing only one of these things, which is why heating curves have sloping and flat sections.
**Energy conservation:** the energy transferred to the system equals the increase in internal energy (if no energy is lost to the surroundings).
core.p: The AQA spec states that **heating changes the energy stored within the system by increasing the energy of the particles that make up the system**. This has one of two effects: it either **raises the temperature** of the system, or it **produces a change of state**. Both increase the internal energy but in different ways.

bullets: Slope: KE increases, PE roughly unchanged (for a given state).
Plateau: PE increases, KE constant.
The **total** internal energy rises everywhere on the graph as long as energy is supplied.
A cooling curve is the reverse: internal energy falls throughout.
The plateau at the boiling point is longer than at the melting point, since far more potential energy change is needed to separate particles entirely.
Link to the **latent heat** point: the energy supplied during a plateau is E = m L.
core.h: Heating curves: kinetic versus potential energy
core.p: A heating curve shows both ideas at once. On the sloping sections the substance is in a single state and its temperature rises, so the **kinetic energy of the particles increases**. On the flat sections, the temperature is constant, so the average kinetic energy is constant, and the energy supplied is increasing the **potential energy** as the particles are separated. Throughout the whole graph the **internal energy continues to rise**.

bullets: **Greater mass:** the same energy is shared between more particles, so each gains less, and the temperature rise is smaller.
**Greater energy input:** a larger temperature rise (directly proportional).

**Material:** a substance with a **higher specific heat capacity** needs more energy per kilogram for each °C, so it warms more slowly. Water (4200 J/kg°C) warms slowly compared with copper (about 385 J/kg°C).
**Equation:** change in thermal energy = mass × specific heat capacity × temperature change, written ΔE = m c Δθ.
**Units:** E in joules (J), m in kilograms (kg), c in J/kg°C, Δθ in °C.
**Rearrangements:** c = ΔE ÷ (m Δθ); Δθ = ΔE ÷ (m c); m = ΔE ÷ (c Δθ).
core.p: When a system is heated and its temperature rises (with no change of state), the size of the rise depends on three things stated in the specification: the **mass** of the substance heated, the **type of material** (its specific heat capacity), and the **energy input** to the system. These are combined in the equation for specific heat capacity.

bullets: Water: c = 4200 J/kg°C, a very high value, which is why water is used for central heating and why coastal areas have a milder climate.
Copper: c ≈ 385 J/kg°C; so it heats and cools quickly (good for kettle bases and pans).
If the system gains energy, ΔE is positive and the temperature rises; if it loses energy ΔE is negative.

**Required practical (specific heat capacity):** heat a block with an immersion heater, measure the current, p.d. and time, calculate E = V I t, and the temperature rise using a thermometer in the block. **Insulate** the block to reduce energy loss; the reading is lower than the true value if energy is lost.
**Power link:** electrical energy E = P t, so the time for a given temperature rise is t = ΔE ÷ P.
core.p: **Specific heat capacity** is the amount of energy required to raise the temperature of **one kilogram** of the substance by **one degree Celsius**. Use ΔE = m c Δθ whenever a substance warms or cools without changing state. Be careful with units: convert grams to kilograms first.

bullets: **Internal energy** (J) is the **total** KE + PE of all particles; it depends on the quantity of material as well as the temperature and state.
**Thermal energy transfer ('heating')** is the process of energy moving from a hotter object to a colder one.
A spark has a very high temperature but a tiny internal energy; a swimming pool is at low temperature but has enormous internal energy.
Energy always transfers from a **higher temperature** region to a **lower temperature** one until thermal equilibrium.
core.h: Temperature versus internal energy versus heat
core.p: These three terms are used loosely in everyday language but have specific scientific meanings. Examiners will not accept 'heat' used as if it were a store of energy. **Temperature** (°C) is a measure of the **average kinetic energy** of the particles; it does not depend on the quantity of material.

bullets: **Conduction** mainly in solids: particles vibrate more and pass kinetic energy on by collisions (and free electrons in metals).
**Convection** in liquids and gases: warmer, less dense fluid rises.
**Radiation:** infrared transferred by electromagnetic waves.
**Electrical heating:** work done by the current in a resistor increases the internal energy of the heater, which then heats the surroundings.
If energy is **lost to the surroundings** (not insulated) the temperature rise is smaller than predicted.
The energy supplied is **conserved**: it is stored in the system or dissipated to the surroundings.
core.h: Energy transfers: conduction, convection, radiation, and work
core.p: Energy can be transferred into or out of a system by several routes, all of which change internal energy. In conduction, vibrating particles pass energy to neighbours; in convection, heated fluid rises and carries energy; in radiation, infrared waves carry energy with no particles. Electrical work from a heater also raises internal energy.

bullets: **Specific latent heat (4.3.2.3):** E = m L is the energy to change state without a temperature change.
**Gas pressure (4.3.3):** raising the temperature of a gas raises the average KE of the particles and hence the pressure in a fixed volume.
**Energy stores (4.1):** the thermal store is the internal energy of the system.
**Electricity (4.2):** E = P t = V I t for heaters.
**Chemistry:** exothermic and endothermic reactions are changes in internal energy of reacting chemicals and surroundings.
core.p: Internal energy joins several areas of the physics course, so expect it to appear in questions that mix topics. **Changes of state (4.3.1):** the PE changes explain constant temperature during melting and boiling.

exam: **Definition (2 marks):** 'the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in a system'. Both kinetic and potential must be named.

**Explain a plateau (2 to 3 marks):** the energy supplied increases the **potential energy** of the particles (overcomes forces between them) while the **kinetic energy and temperature stay constant**.
**Explain a temperature rise (2 marks):** energy transferred increases the **kinetic energy** of the particles so they move faster.
**Calculations (3 marks):** write the equation ΔE = m c Δθ (1), substitute with kg (1), answer with unit J (1). Show working to gain error-carried-forward marks.
**Rearranging:** be ready to find mass, Δθ, c or time (using E = P t).
**Practical questions:** reasons for insulating the container, stirring liquid for even temperature, and using a thermometer in a hole filled with water or oil for good thermal contact.
**Compare questions:** 'same temperature but more internal energy because more particles'.
**Graphs:** from a heating curve, find the plateau temperature and explain the sloping sections using KE and the flat sections using PE.
**6 mark:** link the definition, KE and PE, temperature change versus change of state, and equations for a complete argument.
**Units:** J for energy, kg for mass, °C for temperature change, J/kg°C for specific heat capacity.

mistakes.r: Internal energy is the total kinetic energy AND potential energy of all the particles.
mistakes.w: Internal energy is just the kinetic energy of the particles.

mistakes.r: Temperature is a measure of average kinetic energy; heating is energy transfer; internal energy is the total energy of the particles.
mistakes.w: Heat and temperature are the same.

mistakes.r: Energy is still supplied; it increases the potential energy (separating particles), not the kinetic energy.
mistakes.w: Temperature stays constant because no energy is being supplied.

mistakes.r: Heating either raises the temperature or produces a change of state.
A bigger object has more internal energy but not necessarily a higher temperature.
mistakes.w: A bigger object always has a higher temperature.
Using mass in grams in ΔE = m c Δθ.

mistakes.r: That is kinetic energy of the object. Internal energy is the energy of the particles inside it.
mistakes.w: Internal energy is energy of the whole object moving.

mistakes.r: State that energy is lost to the surroundings, so use insulation; the calculated c is higher than the true value.
mistakes.w: Ignoring energy losses in the specific heat capacity practical.

summary: AQA 4.3.2 requires you to know that energy is stored inside a system by its particles, that **internal energy** is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles, and that heating a system increases the energy of its particles so that either the **temperature rises or the state changes**. You also need the factors that affect a temperature rise (mass, substance, energy input). It underpins specific heat capacity, latent heat and gas pressure questions.

terms.d: An object or group of objects being studied.
The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles (atoms and molecules) that make up a system.
Energy due to the movement of the particles; the average determines the temperature.
Energy stored because of the forces between the particles and their separation.
A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles of a substance.
Energy transfer that increases the energy of the particles of a system; raises temperature or changes the state.
The amount of energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a substance by one degree Celsius.
Physical change between solid, liquid and gas, where the internal energy changes but the temperature stays constant.
The energy store that changes when a system is heated; the internal energy of the particles.
The rate of energy transfer; P = E ÷ t, measured in watts (W).
Energy transfer by vibrating particles passing energy on to neighbouring particles.
The state in which two objects in contact are at the same temperature, so there is no net energy transfer.
Material that reduces energy transfer to the surroundings, so the temperature rise is closer to the theoretical value.

worked.q: A kettle heats 2.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 50 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg°C. Calculate the energy transferred to the water. (3 marks)
A 2000 W heater supplies the energy in the previous question with no energy losses. Calculate the time taken. (2 marks)
steps: E = P t, so t = E ÷ P.

worked.q: A 0.50 kg copper block (c = 385 J/kg°C) gains 15 400 J. It starts at 20 °C. Calculate its final temperature. (3 marks)
